nations.label: Scotland
nations.peer_note: All 32 councils are unitary authorities, so each is compared with the others. The three island councils (Orkney, Shetland, Na h-Eileanan Siar) are very sparsely populated and cost more per resident for most services.
notes: Figures are net revenue expenditure by service (gross service expenditure minus service income), general fund, from councils' audited accounts where available, as defined by the Scottish Government's Local Financial Return.
Social work spending is after income from Integration Joint Boards (IJBs), through which councils and NHS boards jointly run adult social care, so it is not comparable with England or Wales.
Housing is non-HRA housing only (housing benefit administration and homelessness); council housing is paid for from the separate housing revenue account (HRA), shown separately.
Trading services (for example leisure or building services run commercially) can be negative because they earn more than they cost.

nations.label: Wales

services.label: Libraries, culture, heritage, sport and recreation
Council fund housing and housing benefit
Law and order and protective services (older years)

nations.peer_note: All 22 councils are unitary authorities, so each is compared with the others.
notes: Figures are the Welsh Government's revenue outturn expenditure by service for the 22 unitary councils (what they actually spent), from the Revenue Outturn (RO) return, in £ thousand. Fire, police and national park authorities are not included.
Education is spent on schools and related services run by the council; it is shown per child aged 0-17.
Housing and housing benefit and council tax benefit are large because they include benefits paid out and later recovered from central government.

nations.label: Northern Ireland
nations.peer_note: All 11 councils are compared with each other. Belfast is by far the largest council and the only city with the services of a capital.
notes: Northern Ireland's councils are much smaller than councils in the rest of the UK in what they do: they do not run education, social care, housing or roads (these are run by Northern Ireland departments). Their services are mainly waste, leisure and recreation, economic development, planning, building control, cemeteries and community services.

The Department for Communities publishes no council spending by service, and no actual outturn. These figures are each council's estimated net expenditure on services for the rate year, set when district rates are fixed (Table 3 of the annual rate statistics circular). They are plans, not what was actually spent.

For actual spending by service, each council's own audited accounts are the official source; the Local Government Auditor's annual report (NI Audit Office) gives Northern Ireland totals by service category.
